A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RPS research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original RPS-versus-baseline experiments across three models and three datasets in Tables 3–4, together with qualitative case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains these experiments and adds human and Claude evaluations, hyperparameter ablations, projection-correlation measurements, and runtime results.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains neighborhood construction, one response per neighboring direction, and selection by the original target's projected reward. Appendix A.3 adds a geometric neighborhood example supporting the theory; it does not report changing the implemented RPS procedure.

E1.justification: The three datasets and helpfulness–verbosity task remain unchanged. However, v3's ablations refer to eight directions labeled v3–v10, while its direction specifications still define only v1–v8. Whether this represents additional preference scenarios or inconsistent relabeling cannot be established.

E2.justification: Both versions compare RPS against the same target-direction best-of-k baseline using the same DPA, DPO, and SFT models. Human raters and Claude are additional evaluators, not new competing methods.

E3.justification: The original evaluation settings remain, but v3 adds human judging with three-worker majority voting, Claude judging, neighborhood-size and radius sweeps, and synthetic 5°/10° projection tests. Appendix A.15 also introduces resource profiling on 100 HelpSteer2 prompts at two directions. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v3 adds explicit sensitivity tests for k and angular radius, an empirical local-consistency check, and measured computational-overhead analysis in Appendices A.6, A.11, and A.15. Human and second-judge evaluations additionally examine dependence on the original judge. The earlier directional analyses and qualitative cases are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix A.5 newly reports three independent Claude evaluation passes with run-wise mean and standard deviation, and discloses that GPT-4o-mini runs once per model–dataset–direction configuration. The original cross-direction standard deviations and fixed A/B randomization seed remain; this does not establish additional runs of the original generation experiments.

E6.justification: The original Tables 3–4 and case-study outcomes are unchanged. Substantial new results include human v8 win rates of 72.1%, 50.4%, and 85.5% for DPA, DPO, and SFT; Claude scores; correlation and ablation tables; and resource measurements. These are additional evaluations, not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendices A.2–A.3 add an explicit stochastic-dominance assumption, a Lipschitz local-consistency condition with a bounded-reward derivation, a formal d-dimensional Theorem 2, and a 2(d−1)-direction tangent-space construction. These substantially extend the assumptions and mathematical arguments beyond v1's informal consistency approximation. The original maximum-CDF and corollary proofs remain.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion qualify theoretical superiority as conditional on better-trained neighboring directions and local score consistency. The training-free contribution, three-paradigm applicability, and headline win-rate claim remain unchanged. This narrows the presentation of the guarantee without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 3.3 newly identifies abrupt preference changes, including hard safety thresholds, and overly large neighborhoods as regimes where RPS should be treated as a heuristic. The conclusion acknowledges unresolved high-dimensional scaling, and Section 5.2 interprets the new sensitivity and independent-judge evidence. These materially expand applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 adds AMT instructions and interface, worker eligibility and payment information, and A100-class hardware and profiling details. Its reproducibility statement supplies a different repository address, although the introduction retains the old address. Existing generation, judge, and reward-model prompt contents are preserved; repository availability cannot be verified from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v3 adds Zhu et al.'s data-credibility work and removes several introductory and RLHF citations, including Guo et al. (2024) and Zhang et al. (2025). The positioning relative to DPA, DPO, and inference-time steering remains essentially unchanged. Numerous other bibliography edits update metadata for retained works.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. v3 makes localized revisions to the abstract, theory discussion, results discussion, and conclusion; expands and renumbers the appendix; and updates author/header information and acknowledgments. The added scientific material does not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v3 adds dedicated tables for human evaluation, Claude aggregate and directional results, correlations, two ablations, and resource profiling. It also places prompts in labeled shaded boxes and restyles or relocates existing displays. The six original figures are retained, with a qualified Figure 3 caption and relocated Figure 6.

improvement.justification: Human and Claude checks, sensitivity tests, and resource measurements strengthen the empirical basis beyond v1's single-judge evaluation, while explicit failure conditions improve interpretation. The net gain is limited: Appendix A.2 still does not establish that own-direction stochastic dominance survives bounded projection error, and Section 3.3's new correlation summary conflicts with Table 8 at 10°. Undefined ablation direction labels also limit reproducibility.
